quiz.e: Journalists must balance discoverability with the ethical duty not to mislead readers through sensationalized framing.

quiz.q: Why is metadata checking useful in verifying a photo or video's authenticity?
o: Metadata can reveal information like the date, location, or device used, helping confirm or challenge a claimed origin
Metadata automatically proves whether a file was edited, so it settles authenticity in a single check
Metadata is permanently locked and cannot be viewed by anyone other than the platform that hosts the file
Metadata is stripped from every file, so it can never provide clues about when or where something was captured
quiz.e: Examining metadata is one tool among several (alongside reverse image search) for authenticating digital content.

quiz.q: What is a common newsroom guideline for staff personal social media accounts?
o: Post as often as possible about covered topics, since a strong personal brand helps the newsroom's reach
Avoid social media completely, since any online account is a violation of professional standards
Share unconfirmed tips right away, since speed on social platforms matters more than checking claims
Avoid publicly stating personal opinions on topics they professionally cover, to protect perceived objectivity
quiz.e: Many outlets restrict staff commentary on covered topics to preserve the newsroom's credibility and impartiality.

quiz.q: Which best illustrates responsible verification of a viral video before republishing it?
o: Relying on view counts and shares to decide that it is genuine, since popular clips are rarely fake
Trusting the account that posted it if that user has many followers and a verified badge on the platform
Asking the uploader to confirm it is real in a comment, then publishing once they reply
Using reverse image/video search and checking metadata to confirm its date, location, and authenticity
quiz.e: Popularity does not indicate accuracy; verification tools should be used regardless of how widely a video has spread.

quiz.q: How should a corrected error in a digital article ideally be disclosed?
o: By silently replacing the wrong text so the page reads cleanly, with no mention that a change was made
By removing the article from the website so readers cannot see the original mistake or its fix
With a visible, timestamped correction note explaining what changed
By notifying only the person named in the error, without any public note for the wider audience
quiz.e: Transparent correction practices maintain reader trust and distinguish honest journalism from unacknowledged editing.

quiz.q: What is one advantage of pairing text reporting with an explanatory video for a complex story?
o: Video can visually demonstrate a process or event that is difficult to convey in text alone
Video completely replaces written text, so a story needs no article once footage has been published
Video removes the duty to verify facts, since viewers can see events for themselves on screen
Video is demanded by search engine guidelines, which require a clip to be included with every story
quiz.e: Different formats serve different strengths — video for visual demonstration, text for depth and nuance — often used together.

quiz.q: Why do journalists need updated verification tools for the era of AI-generated content?
o: Traditional methods of judging authenticity by appearance alone are less reliable against sophisticated AI fabrications
Creators of AI content are required to label it clearly, so audiences can always tell it from real footage
AI-generated media can never be checked by any method, so newsrooms must refuse to use anything suspicious
Synthetic content is too uncommon to matter, so existing habits of visual inspection remain fully adequate
quiz.e: As synthetic media becomes more convincing, newsrooms need dedicated tools and training to detect manipulation.

quiz.q: What does 'search engine results page' (SERP) placement typically depend on?
o: A lottery run by the search engine, with each page given a position by chance for every query
Mostly the word count of the article, with longer pieces always ranking above shorter ones
Relevance, structure, and quality signals like keywords, metadata, and site authority
The number of followers the writer has on personal social accounts, which sets the page's order
quiz.e: Search engines rank pages based on relevance and quality signals, which is why clear structure and metadata matter for SEO.

quiz.q: Which best explains why journalists should be cautious about content 'aggregated' from social media without direct verification?
o: Aggregated content may be unverified, mislabeled, or taken out of its original context
Platforms check and certify every post before it appears, so aggregated items are already fully confirmed
Once content is credited to its social media source, the outlet carries no responsibility for errors in it
Social networks legally guarantee the accuracy of everything users upload, so reposting poses no risk
quiz.e: Platforms do not guarantee accuracy, so outlets remain responsible for verifying anything they republish or reference.

quiz.q: What is the primary purpose of combining data journalism with interactive visualization?
o: To slow down page loading so that readers spend more time on the site and see more advertisements
To let readers explore and understand data-driven findings directly, beyond what a static chart or narrative can convey
To make written narrative unnecessary, since charts and graphics alone are enough to explain any story
To meet a legal requirement that public-records laws place on any story built from government figures
quiz.e: Interactivity allows readers to engage directly with the underlying data, deepening understanding beyond a static presentation.

PART_A.q: Which news value refers to how many people are affected by an event and how seriously?
o: Impact/consequence
Timeliness
Novelty
Proximity
PART_A.e: Impact measures the scale and seriousness of an event's effect on the audience.

PART_A.q: What does 'agenda-setting' theory claim about the press?
o: The media shapes what audiences think about, not necessarily what to think
The media has no influence on public opinion
The media only reports facts with zero selection bias
Agenda-setting only applies to opinion journalism
PART_A.e: Agenda-setting theory holds that prominence in coverage signals importance to the public, even without persuasion.

PART_A.q: What is the primary purpose of the inverted pyramid structure?
o: To present the most newsworthy information first, in case readers stop reading
To build suspense toward a dramatic ending
To organize a story chronologically
To separate fact from opinion
PART_A.e: The inverted pyramid front-loads the most important facts so readers get the key information even if they stop reading early.

PART_A.q: What are the 'Five Ws and H' used for in news writing?
o: Ensuring a story answers who, what, when, where, why, and how
Formatting a headline
Structuring an editorial's argument
Citing legal sources
PART_A.e: The Five Ws and H are the essential questions a complete news story should answer.

PART_A.q: What is the purpose of an open-ended question in an interview?
o: To encourage a detailed, expansive response rather than a yes/no answer
To confirm a fact quickly
To end the interview
To avoid follow-up questions
PART_A.e: Open-ended questions invite subjects to elaborate, producing richer material than closed yes/no questions.

PART_A.q: What does it mean for a source to speak 'on background'?
o: Information can be used but not attributed to the source by name
The interview is entirely off the record
The source must be quoted verbatim
The conversation is recorded for legal purposes only
PART_A.e: On background allows use of the information without directly naming the source, per an agreed arrangement.

PART_A.q: What is the core principle of fact-checking in journalism?
o: Verifying claims against independent, reliable evidence before publication
Trusting any single source without corroboration
Publishing first and correcting errors later as routine practice
Only checking facts that seem controversial
PART_A.e: Fact-checking requires independent verification of claims before a story is published.

PART_A.q: What is plagiarism in a journalism context?
o: Presenting someone else's words or reporting as your own without attribution
Quoting a source with proper attribution
Paraphrasing a press release with credit
Citing a public record
PART_A.e: Plagiarism is using another's work without giving credit, a serious ethical violation in journalism.

PART_A.q: What is the purpose of a nut graf in a feature story?
o: To explain why the story matters after the narrative opening
To conclude the story with a summary
To introduce the reporter
To list the story's sources
PART_A.e: The nut graf tells readers the significance of the story after an anecdotal or narrative lede.

PART_A.q: Which best describes 'show, don't tell' in feature writing?
o: Using concrete sensory detail rather than abstract description
Avoiding all quotes
Writing only in the passive voice
Never describing a physical setting
PART_A.e: Specific, sensory detail creates more vivid and credible scenes than vague, abstract language.

PART_A.q: What distinguishes an editorial from a news article?
o: An editorial represents the publication's institutional opinion, while news reports facts
An editorial is always signed by one reporter
News articles always include the reporter's opinion
There is no meaningful distinction
PART_A.e: Editorials are unsigned, institutional opinion pieces, separate from objective news reporting.

PART_A.q: What is 'false balance' in news coverage?
o: Giving a fringe or unsupported claim equal weight to a well-evidenced position
Reporting only one side of an issue
Never including any opinion content
Balancing a story's word count evenly between sources
PART_A.e: False balance misleads readers by treating a weak claim as equally credible as strong evidence.

PART_A.q: What is the difference between libel and slander?
o: Libel is written defamation; slander is spoken defamation
Libel is spoken; slander is written
They are legally identical terms
Libel applies only to broadcast media
PART_A.e: Libel refers to defamation in written or published form; slander refers to spoken defamation.

PART_A.q: What must a public official prove to win a defamation case?
o: Actual malice — knowledge of falsity or reckless disregard for the truth
Simple negligence
Nothing beyond the statement being false
That the reporter disliked them
PART_A.e: New York Times v. Sullivan established the actual malice standard for public officials and figures.

PART_A.q: What is the main goal of SEO in journalism?
o: Structuring content so it is more easily found by search engines and readers
Making headlines as sensational as possible
Removing keywords from articles
Avoiding metadata entirely
PART_A.e: SEO helps accurate journalism reach readers who are actively searching for relevant information.

PART_A.q: Why should content found on social media be verified before republication?
o: Being publicly posted does not make content automatically authentic or accurate
Social media content is always accurate
Verification only applies to print stories
Social posts cannot legally be referenced
PART_A.e: Social media content requires the same verification standard as any other source before being republished.

PART_A.q: What is the difference between hard news and soft news?
o: Hard news covers timely, significant events; soft news covers lifestyle and human-interest topics
Hard news is always shorter than soft news
Soft news requires more fact-checking than hard news
There is no meaningful difference
PART_A.e: Hard news covers urgent, significant events like crime and politics; soft news covers lifestyle and human-interest topics with less time pressure.

PART_A.q: What is a lede in news writing?
o: The opening sentence or paragraph that presents the most important information
The story's headline
The reporter's byline
The final paragraph of a story
PART_A.e: The lede is the crucial opening that conveys the story's most newsworthy information.

PART_A.q: Why is active listening important during an interview?
o: It allows the reporter to ask meaningful follow-up questions based on what the subject actually says
It ensures the reporter never takes notes
It replaces the need for preparation
It guarantees the source will avoid controversial topics
PART_A.e: Active listening lets a reporter follow up on unexpected or important details rather than sticking rigidly to a prepared list.

PART_A.q: What is a conflict of interest in journalism ethics?
o: A situation where a reporter's personal interests could compromise objective reporting
A disagreement between two sources
A type of investigative story
A legal claim against a publication
PART_A.e: Conflicts of interest arise when personal relationships or interests could bias a reporter's coverage.

PART_A.q: What is a 'kicker' in a feature story?
o: The strong closing line, quote, or image that ends the story with resonance
The opening paragraph
The story's headline
A type of fact-check
PART_A.e: The kicker is the memorable final element chosen to leave a lasting impression.

PART_A.q: What is an op-ed?
o: A signed opinion piece by someone outside the publication's staff
An unsigned institutional opinion piece
A straight news story
A press release
PART_A.e: Op-eds are attributed to an outside writer, distinguishing them from unsigned editorials.

PART_A.q: What is the purpose of a shield law?
o: To protect journalists from being legally compelled to reveal confidential sources
To require reporters to reveal all sources
To shield officials from press scrutiny
To block all lawsuits against news organizations
PART_A.e: Shield laws protect source confidentiality so information can flow to reporters without fear of exposure.

PART_A.q: What is a deepfake?
o: AI-generated or manipulated video or audio that convincingly depicts events that did not occur
A verified, authentic photo
A type of SEO metadata
A synonym for a live blog
PART_A.e: Deepfakes present a growing verification challenge because they can convincingly fabricate video or audio.

PART_A.q: What is gatekeeping in journalism?
o: The process by which editors decide which stories reach the public
A legal term for defamation defenses
A type of interview technique
A synonym for fact-checking
PART_A.e: Gatekeeping happens at every editorial stage, determining what stories are covered and published.

PART_A.q: What information typically belongs in the nut graf of a hard news story?
o: Why the story matters and its broader context
The reporter's personal opinion
A detailed physical description of the setting
The story's final conclusion
PART_A.e: In hard news, the nut graf situates the lede within its broader significance and context.

PART_A.q: What is the benefit of preparing research before an interview?
o: It allows the reporter to ask more informed, specific questions
It eliminates the need for follow-up questions
It guarantees the source will not lie
It replaces the need for fact-checking afterward
PART_A.e: Background research helps reporters ask sharper questions and recognize when an answer needs further probing.

PART_A.q: Why do reputable news organizations issue corrections?
o: To maintain accuracy and transparency after publishing an error
To avoid legal liability entirely
Because corrections are optional and rarely used
To replace the need for fact-checking before publication
PART_A.e: Corrections uphold journalistic accountability by transparently fixing published errors.

PART_A.q: What type of feature identifies a pattern occurring across many people or places?
o: A trend story
A profile
A kicker
An editorial
PART_A.e: Trend stories illustrate a broader pattern using multiple examples, distinct from a single-subject profile.

PART_A.q: What is a column, as distinct from an editorial or op-ed?
o: A recurring, signed opinion piece reflecting one writer's consistent viewpoint
An unsigned institutional statement
A one-time guest submission
A straight news report
PART_A.e: Columns run regularly under one writer's byline, unlike unsigned editorials or one-off op-eds.

PART_B1.q: [Application] A local paper covers a minor traffic accident because the driver is a famous actor. Which news value is most responsible for this becoming a story?
o: Prominence
Timeliness
Proximity
Oddity
PART_B1.e: A well-known person's involvement makes an otherwise minor event newsworthy — the definition of prominence.

PART_B1.q: [Application] A hard news story about a factory fire buries the number of injuries in the seventh paragraph. What structural principle has been violated?
o: The inverted pyramid, which requires the most important facts first
The Five Ws and H, which requires alphabetical order
The nut graf rule, which only applies to features
The AP Style rule on numerals
PART_B1.e: Key facts like casualties belong near the top under inverted pyramid structure, not buried deep in the story.

PART_B1.q: [Application] A source suddenly reveals an unexpected, important detail mid-interview that the reporter had not planned to ask about. What should the reporter do?
o: Follow up with clarifying questions based on active listening, even if it departs from the prepared list
Ignore it and continue with the prepared questions only
End the interview immediately
Refuse to include it in the story regardless of relevance
PART_B1.e: Active listening means adapting the interview to pursue newsworthy details as they emerge.

PART_B1.q: [Application] A reporter has one anonymous source for a serious allegation against a public official. What is the best practice before publishing?
o: Seek independent corroboration from additional sources or documents
Publish immediately since one source is always sufficient
Wait for the official to confirm the allegation personally
Rely solely on the source's reputation for honesty
PART_B1.e: Serious claims generally require corroboration beyond a single anonymous source to meet verification standards.

PART_B1.q: [Application] A feature story opens with a vivid scene of a nurse comforting a patient, then in paragraph three explains that the story is really about a nationwide nursing shortage. What is paragraph three functioning as?
o: The nut graf
The kicker
The dateline
The headline
PART_B1.e: The paragraph that reveals why the story matters, after the narrative opening, is the nut graf.

PART_B1.q: [Application] A news article about a new policy uses the word 'controversial regime' instead of 'government.' What issue does this illustrate?
o: Loaded language that may signal bias
A correctly balanced report
A properly labeled editorial
An example of actual malice
PART_B1.e: Word choices like 'regime' carry connotations that can bias a supposedly neutral news report.

PART_B1.q: [Application] A newspaper publishes a leaked but authentic classified document. The government seeks a court order to stop further distribution before it's fully published. What legal doctrine is most relevant?
o: Prior restraint, which courts treat as presumptively unconstitutional
Actual malice, which applies only to defamation
FOIA exemptions, which apply only to record requests
Shield law protections, which apply only to sources
PART_B1.e: Blocking publication in advance is prior restraint, which the Supreme Court has held requires an extremely high burden to justify.

PART_B1.q: [Application] A reporter finds a dramatic photo circulating on social media claiming to show a local disaster. What should they do before using it?
o: Run a reverse image search and verify its date, location, and source
Publish it immediately since it is already public
Assume it is authentic because it has many shares
Credit it to 'social media' without further checking
PART_B1.e: Verification tools like reverse image search are essential before republishing unconfirmed social media content.

PART_B1.q: [Synthesis] How do news values and gatekeeping work together to shape what audiences see?
o: Editors apply news values to select stories, and that selection itself sets the public agenda
News values determine legal liability, while gatekeeping determines story length
Gatekeeping eliminates the need for news values
News values apply only to soft news, gatekeeping only to hard news
PART_B1.e: Gatekeepers use news values to choose stories, and those choices shape which topics gain public attention (agenda-setting).

PART_B1.q: [Synthesis] Why does the inverted pyramid structure support both readers and editors?
o: It lets readers get key facts quickly and lets editors cut from the bottom without losing essential information
It guarantees a story will never need editing
It replaces the need for headlines
It only benefits editors, not readers
PART_B1.e: Because information is ordered by importance, editors can trim length from the end while preserving the core facts for readers.

PART_B1.q: [Synthesis] How does thorough pre-interview research connect to effective fact-checking later?
o: Good research helps reporters ask precise questions and recognize inconsistencies that need later verification
Research replaces the need for any fact-checking
Fact-checking only applies to written documents, not interviews
Research and fact-checking are unrelated processes
PART_B1.e: Preparation sharpens interview questions and helps reporters flag claims that will require independent verification.

PART_B1.q: [Synthesis] Why do transparency and corrections matter to maintaining public trust in journalism?
o: Openly acknowledging and fixing errors demonstrates a commitment to accuracy over image
Corrections make a publication appear less credible
Trust depends only on speed of publication
Transparency is only relevant to opinion journalism
PART_B1.e: Visible accountability for mistakes, rather than hiding them, is central to maintaining journalistic credibility.

PART_B1.q: [Synthesis] How does descriptive detail support the overall goals of narrative structure in a feature?
o: Specific, sensory detail brings scenes to life, helping the narrative arc engage readers emotionally
Description is unrelated to a feature's structure
Vague description strengthens narrative pacing better than specific detail
Descriptive detail is only used in the kicker
PART_B1.e: Concrete, sensory detail supports the scene-by-scene storytelling that narrative feature structures depend on.

PART_B1.q: [Synthesis] Why is the separation between editorial boards and newsrooms important for maintaining objectivity?
o: It prevents the publication's institutional opinions from shaping supposedly neutral news reporting
It eliminates the need for fact-checking in opinion content
It means editorials are illegal
It ensures reporters never have personal opinions
PART_B1.e: The wall of separation protects the news desk's independence from the outlet's institutional stances.

PART_B1.q: [Synthesis] How do shield laws and the actual malice standard both serve free press values, despite addressing different issues?
o: Both provide legal breathing room — shield laws protect sources, and actual malice protects vigorous reporting on public figures
Both are federal laws automatically covering every journalist
Both eliminate the need for factual accuracy
Both apply exclusively to broadcast journalism
PART_B1.e: Though distinct doctrines, both reduce legal risk in ways that support robust, independent journalism.

PART_B1.q: [Synthesis] How does SEO best practice align with journalism ethics, when done correctly?
o: Clear, accurate, keyword-relevant headlines serve both discoverability and honesty, unlike clickbait
SEO always requires sacrificing accuracy for clicks
Ethics and SEO can never be reconciled
SEO applies only to opinion content
PART_B1.e: Good SEO practice — accurate, descriptive headlines and structure — reinforces rather than undermines ethical standards.

PART_B1.q: [Synthesis] How do the Five Ws and H relate to the inverted pyramid's opening paragraphs?
o: The most critical Ws (who, what, when, where) are typically answered in the lede, with why and how following
The Five Ws and H apply only to feature writing, not hard news
The inverted pyramid ignores the Five Ws entirely
Why and how must always appear before who and what
PART_B1.e: The lede typically covers the core facts (who, what, when, where), while why and how can be developed shortly after.

PART_B1.q: [Synthesis] How does avoiding conflicts of interest support the broader goal of objectivity discussed elsewhere in the course?
o: Both aim to keep personal factors from shaping how facts are reported
Conflicts of interest are unrelated to objectivity
Objectivity requires reporters to have financial stakes in their stories
Avoiding conflicts of interest only matters in opinion writing
PART_B1.e: Managing conflicts of interest is one concrete way reporters uphold the broader standard of objective reporting.

PART_B1.q: [Synthesis] How does the fact-versus-opinion distinction connect to avoiding false balance?
o: Recognizing that opinions and unsupported claims are not facts helps journalists avoid presenting them as equally credible to well-evidenced facts
Fact-checking makes false balance impossible by definition
Opinions are always facts once published
False balance only concerns editorials, not news
PART_B1.e: Understanding the fact/opinion distinction helps journalists weigh evidence properly rather than treating unsupported claims as equally valid.

PART_B1.q: [Synthesis] Why is verification particularly critical in the era of deepfakes and AI-generated content, connecting to fact-checking principles from earlier units?
o: The core fact-checking obligation to verify claims before publishing now extends to verifying the authenticity of digital media itself
Fact-checking principles do not apply to visual or audio content
AI-generated content is always self-labeled, so no extra verification is needed
Verification is now less important since technology has improved accuracy
PART_B1.e: The traditional duty to verify claims now must extend to authenticating video, audio, and images against sophisticated fabrication.

PART_B2.q: [Synthesis] A story about a small local election spreads nationally after a viral clip surfaces from the event. Which combination of news values best explains its unexpected reach?
o: Novelty/oddity combined with the viral spread accelerating the news cycle
Proximity alone, since it is a local story
Prominence, because local candidates are always famous
Impact, because local elections always affect millions
PART_B2.e: An unusual, viral moment (novelty) combined with rapid digital spread illustrates how the news cycle can elevate a local story nationally.

PART_B2.q: [Synthesis] A reporter interviewing a grieving family for a feature must balance sensitivity with the need for authentic detail. Which principle from interviewing and feature writing units applies here?
o: Building trust and rapport while still gathering concrete, honest detail for the story
Avoiding all direct quotes to protect the family
Skipping the interview since sensitive topics cannot be reported
Only using information from official police reports
PART_B2.e: Ethical interviewing balances compassion with the reporting rigor needed for an authentic feature.

PART_B2.q: [Synthesis] A wire service story and a local feature both cover the same disaster. How would their structures likely differ?
o: The wire story likely uses the inverted pyramid for speed, while the feature may use a narrative arc for emotional depth
Both must use identical structures under AP style
The feature must appear before the wire story
Wire stories never include the Five Ws
PART_B2.e: Straight news favors the inverted pyramid for speed and clarity, while features often use narrative structures for emotional engagement.

PART_B2.q: [Synthesis] A publication corrects a factual error within an hour of publishing and clearly labels the correction. How does this reflect the ethical standards discussed across the course?
o: It demonstrates the transparency and accuracy standards expected of both hard news and feature journalism
Corrections are only required for opinion content
Fast corrections indicate poor initial fact-checking and nothing else
Labeling corrections is optional under most ethics codes
PART_B2.e: Prompt, transparent correction reflects the accountability standard that applies across all journalism, not just one genre.

PART_B2.q: [Synthesis] An editorial board endorses a candidate while the newsroom continues neutral coverage of the race. What does this arrangement demonstrate?
o: The separation between institutional opinion and objective news reporting
A conflict of interest that violates journalism ethics
Evidence that the newsroom is biased
A rare and improper practice not used by real newspapers
PART_B2.e: This is the standard, ethical structure: editorial opinion and news reporting operate independently within the same publication.

PART_B2.q: [Synthesis] A journalist uses a FOIA request to obtain records revealing a discrepancy from a source's earlier claims. What does this illustrate about combining reporting tools?
o: Public records can independently verify or challenge information gathered through interviews
FOIA requests always contradict source interviews
Sources are unnecessary once FOIA records are obtained
FOIA cannot be used alongside interview-based reporting
PART_B2.e: Combining documentary evidence with interviews strengthens verification, showing how different reporting tools reinforce each other.

PART_B2.q: [Synthesis] A data journalism project uses an interactive map built from a FOIA-obtained dataset. Which two units' concepts does this project combine?
o: Media law (FOIA) and digital storytelling (data visualization)
Interviewing skills and editorial writing only
Feature writing and libel law only
News values and headline SEO only
PART_B2.e: The project draws on media law's FOIA process to obtain data and digital storytelling's visualization techniques to present it.

PART_B2.q: [Synthesis] A feature writer spends three weeks observing a subject before writing, gathering specific sensory details and multiple interviews. How does this reporting process connect to fact-checking standards from earlier units?
o: Extended, careful reporting supports the same rigorous verification standard required of all journalism, not just hard news
Features are exempt from fact-checking due to their narrative style
Observation alone eliminates the need for source interviews
Sensory detail does not need to be factually accurate
PART_B2.e: Even narrative, descriptive reporting must meet the same verification standards as straight news.

PART_B2.q: [Synthesis] A newsroom must decide between covering a novel but minor local event and a high-impact but less unusual national story with limited space. What editorial process determines the choice?
o: Gatekeeping, which weighs competing news values like novelty and impact against available space
FOIA, which only applies to government records
Actual malice, which only applies to defamation
SEO, which only concerns headline wording
PART_B2.e: Editors act as gatekeepers, weighing competing news values to decide what limited space or airtime covers.

PART_B2.q: [Synthesis] A reporter is subpoenaed to reveal a confidential source used in an investigative feature. Which two concepts from the course are most directly in tension here?
o: Shield law protections for sources and the legal risk of contempt of court for refusing to comply
SEO and headline writing
Objectivity and the inverted pyramid
News values and gatekeeping
PART_B2.e: This scenario pits a reporter's ethical/legal commitment to source confidentiality (shield laws) against the legal consequence of contempt for refusing a court order.

PART_C.q: Written response: choose TWO concepts from different units and construct an argument connecting them. Cite specific evidence from each.
o: Names both concepts precisely, gives concrete evidence for each, and explains the causal/logical bridge
Lists the two topics without connecting them
Describes only one concept in detail
Gives a personal opinion with no course evidence
PART_C.e: Strong responses anchor every claim in specific unit content.

PART_C.q: Essay plan: identify the single most important takeaway of this course. Defend it using three units as evidence, then address one counterargument.
o: Clear thesis, three unit-specific pieces of evidence, genuine counterargument, resolution
Thesis with no support
Topic list with no argument
Anecdote unrelated to course content
PART_C.e: Full argumentative architecture earns top marks.

workedExamples.title: Inverted pyramid lead
workedExamples.prompt: Write a lead for: A school board voted 5-2 on Tuesday night to move the start time to 8:30 a.m. next fall, to give students more sleep.
steps: Put the most important facts first: who, what, when
Add why, and keep it to one sentence
workedExamples.answer: The school board voted 5-2 Tuesday to start school at 8:30 a.m. next fall so students can get more sleep.

workedExamples.title: Fact-checking
workedExamples.prompt: A source says 'Crime is up 40%.' What should you check before printing?
steps: Ask for the source of the number
Compare the time period and the baseline
Check official data and get a second source
workedExamples.answer: Verify the data, period and baseline with official records and another source

workedExamples.title: Judging newsworthiness
workedExamples.prompt: A school paper must choose between a story on a new bus schedule and a story on the weather. Which is more newsworthy?
steps: Apply news values: impact, proximity and timeliness.
The bus schedule affects many students' daily routines.
Weather is common knowledge unless it disrupts school.
workedExamples.answer: The bus schedule, because it affects many readers directly.

workedExamples.title: Writing a lede
workedExamples.prompt: Write a lede: the mayor announced a new park, which costs $2 million and opens in June.
steps: List the key facts: who, what, cost and when.
Put the most important and interesting fact first.
Keep it to one or two clear sentences.
workedExamples.answer: Mayor Lee announced a $2 million park that will open in June.

workedExamples.title: Preparing interview questions
workedExamples.prompt: You will interview the principal about a new phone policy. Prepare good questions.
steps: Research the policy first so you don't waste time on basics.
Ask open-ended questions that begin with why or how.
Plan follow-up questions based on the answers.
workedExamples.answer: Why was the policy adopted, and how will it be enforced?

workedExamples.title: Separating fact and opinion
workedExamples.prompt: Is 'The cafeteria food is terrible' a fact or an opinion?
steps: A fact can be verified with evidence or measurement.
'Terrible' is a judgment that varies from person to person.
A verifiable version would be 'Sixty percent of students rated the food below average in a survey.'

workedExamples.title: Is it libel?
workedExamples.prompt: A paper prints a false claim that a local business cheats its customers. Could this be libel?
steps: Libel requires a false statement of fact that is published.
The statement must harm the business's reputation.
Because the claim is false and damaging, the paper could be liable unless a defense applies.
workedExamples.answer: Yes, it could be libel; truth is the strongest defense, and here the claim is false.

workedExamples.title: Writing a feature lead
workedExamples.prompt: Write an anecdotal lead for a feature about a student volunteer at a food bank.
steps: Choose a vivid moment instead of a general statement.
Use sensory or specific detail.
Hint at the larger story to draw the reader in.
workedExamples.answer: At 6 a.m., Maya was already stacking cans at the food bank, long before her first class.
